subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 52-year-old man is hospitalized with fever and chills of 4 days' duration. Auscultation reveals a new blowing systolic murmur at the apex. Examination shows flat, painless, erythematous macules on his palms and soles and linear hemorrhages under several fingernails. Blood cultures are pending.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the lesions on this patient's palms?

options.text: Immune complex deposition in the small vessels of the dermis
Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to bacterial antigens
Direct infiltration of the dermis by circulating bacteria
Septic microembolization of small dermal vessels
Retinal microhemorrhage extending to the palmar skin

explanation_correct: Flat, painless, erythematous lesions on the palms or soles are Janeway lesions, a vascular phenomenon of infective endocarditis caused by septic microembolization of the small dermal vessels. They accompany other vascular phenomena such as petechiae, splinter hemorrhages (linear hemorrhages under the nails, also present here), and septic embolism, and occur alongside the most common presentation of fever and a new murmur.

explanation_incorrect.A: Immune complex deposition accounts for the immunologic phenomena of endocarditis, such as glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, and Roth spots. Osler nodes are painful and raised rather than flat and painless, which distinguishes them from these palmar lesions.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity is a cell-mediated response that produces indurated, delayed skin reactions such as the tuberculin test; it is not the mechanism of Janeway lesions in infective endocarditis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Janeway lesions result from septic emboli lodging in dermal vessels, not from direct bacterial infiltration of the skin; this distinction explains why they are classified with the vascular rather than immunologic phenomena.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers (Roth spots) are immunologic findings seen on fundoscopy, not skin lesions, and hemorrhage of the retina has no relation to palmar macules.

educationalObjective: Janeway lesions are painless, flat, erythematous lesions on the palms or soles caused by septic microembolization and are classified as vascular phenomena of infective endocarditis.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of low-grade fevers, night sweats, fatigue, and weight loss. He underwent routine dental cleaning 5 weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). A new soft holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. Two sets of blood cultures grow small gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative and optochin-resistant.
question: Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?
explanation_correct: This is subacute infective endocarditis: a gradual onset over weeks with low-grade fever and smaller vegetations on an abnormal or damaged valve, classically following a dental procedure that seeded the bloodstream. The causative organism is viridans group streptococcus, a low-virulence, catalase-negative, optochin-resistant, gram-positive coccus in chains, which is the most common cause of subacute disease on previously damaged native valves.

explanation_incorrect.A: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valves and would be catalase-positive, coagulase-negative staphylococci, not the chained, catalase-negative organism grown here, and this patient has no prosthetic material.
explanation_incorrect.C: Enterococcus faecalis follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures; it grows as gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and can grow in 6.5% NaCl, but the setting here is a dental procedure, the classic antecedent of viridans streptococcal endocarditis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S bovis) is associated with colon cancer or colon polyps and GI bacteremia; there is no evidence of colonic disease in this vignette.
explanation_incorrect.E: Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus) is a cause of neonatal meningitis rather than a classic cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures, and its identification features do not match the optochin-resistant, small-chain organism described.

educationalObjective: Subacute infective endocarditis after dental procedures is classically caused by viridans streptococci, which produce small vegetations on previously abnormal valves with gradual onset over weeks.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 28-year-old man who injects opioids intravenously presents with 4 days of high fever and pleuritic chest pain. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). Chest imaging shows multiple peripheral nodular opacities, some with cavitation. A soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border becomes louder with inspiration. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase-positive.
question: Which valve is most likely involved, and which organism is the most likely cause?
explanation_correct: Injection drug use is classically associated with right-sided (tricuspid valve) infective endocarditis — the mnemonic is "don't tri drugs" — and the most common organism is Staphylococcus aureus. The clinical clues are the rapid onset of high fever, a murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (a right-sided murmur), and cavitating pulmonary nodules representing septic emboli to the lungs, which occur with right-sided endocarditis. Coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci in clusters confirm S aureus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae is not the classic organism for endocarditis in injection drug use, and the left-sided aortic valve would produce systemic rather than pulmonary septic emboli.
explanation_incorrect.B: Viridans streptococci cause subacute left-sided endocarditis on abnormal valves after dental procedures, with gradual onset, not the explosive febrile illness with pulmonary septic emboli seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valve endocarditis, is coagulase-negative, and typically affects the mitral or prosthetic valve rather than the right heart of an injection drug user.
explanation_incorrect.E: Although Candida can cause endocarditis in injection drug use, fungal endocarditis is far less common than bacterial disease (bacteria >> fungi), and the cultures here show coagulase-positive cocci in clusters, which identifies S aureus.

educationalObjective: In injection drug use, right-sided (tricuspid) infective endocarditis with pulmonary septic emboli is classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 62-year-old man who raises sheep is evaluated for 6 weeks of intermittent fever, weight loss, and fatigue. Three sets of blood cultures obtained during febrile episodes show no growth after 5 days of incubation. Transthoracic echocardiography shows an 11-mm vegetation on the aortic valve with moderate regurgitation. Serologic testing shows markedly elevated phase I IgG antibodies against an intracellular gram-negative coccobacillus.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation_correct: Culture-negative endocarditis with an exposure to livestock (sheep) and serologic evidence of antibodies to an intracellular gram-negative coccobacillus identifies Coxiella burnetii, the agent of Q fever, one of the two classic culture-negative endocarditis organisms (with Bartonella). Coxiella requires serologic diagnosis because it does not grow in routine blood cultures, matching the negative cultures with a clear echocardiographic vegetation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cardiobacterium hominis is a member of the HACEK group of gram-negative organisms that can cause culture-negative endocarditis, but HACEK organisms are slow-growing rather than truly serology-diagnosed, and this vignette's livestock exposure and phase I IgG serology point specifically to Coxiella.
explanation_incorrect.B: Streptococcus gallolyticus is associated with colon cancer and grows readily in blood cultures, which contradicts the repeatedly negative cultures in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as Staphylococcus epidermidis are associated with prosthetic valves and grow in blood cultures within days; this patient has no prosthetic material and cultures are negative.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bartonella quintana is the other classic culture-negative endocarditis organism, but it is associated with homelessness, alcohol use disorder, and body lice exposure, not livestock; Bartonella henselae is linked to cat exposure, and neither produces the phase I IgG serologic pattern of Coxiella.

educationalObjective: Culture-negative infective endocarditis is classically caused by Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella; Coxiella is suggested by livestock exposure and diagnosed with phase I IgG serology.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 74-year-old man presents with 10 days of fever and malaise, 3 weeks after undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). A new systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains that are catalase-negative and grow in 6.5% NaCl broth.
question: Which of the following is the most likely organism?
explanation_correct: Genitourinary (and gastrointestinal) procedures such as transurethral prostate resection are the classic antecedent of enterococcal infective endocarditis. Enterococcus faecalis is a catalase-negative, gram-positive coccus in pairs and chains, distinguished from streptococci by its ability to grow in 6.5% NaCl (bile esculin positive), exactly matching the culture description. Fever with a new murmur completes the picture of subacute endocarditis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Streptococcus gallolyticus is associated with colon cancer or colonic lesions and would not grow in 6.5% NaCl broth; there is no colonic pathology suggested here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Staphylococcus epidermidis is associated with prosthetic valves and is catalase-positive and coagulase-negative in clusters, not catalase-negative cocci in pairs and chains.
explanation_incorrect.D: Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis and skin infections and is not a classic cause of endocarditis after urologic instrumentation, and it cannot grow in 6.5% NaCl.
explanation_incorrect.E: Eikenella corrodens is a gram-negative HACEK organism associated with human bites and is not a gram-positive coccus growing in high-salt broth.

educationalObjective: Endocarditis following GI or GU procedures is classically caused by Enterococcus, which can be distinguished from streptococci by growth in 6.5% NaCl.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 46-year-old man being treated for mitral valve infective endocarditis suddenly develops left flank pain. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria without dysuria or pyuria. CT of the abdomen shows a wedge-shaped hypodensity in the spleen with no mass or hydronephrosis. Urine culture is negative.
question: Which of the following best explains the findings on this patient's abdominal CT?

options.text: Immune complex deposition in the splenic vasculature
Retrograde spread of infection through the left renal vein
Rupture of a mycotic aneurysm into the splenic parenchyma
Septic embolism from the left-sided valvular vegetation
Direct extension of infection through the pericardium

explanation_correct: Left-sided (mitral or aortic) infective endocarditis sheds septic emboli into the systemic circulation, which can lodge in the spleen, kidneys, brain, or mesenteric vessels and produce wedge-shaped infarcts with sudden pain. The vegetation composed of platelets, fibrin, and microbes can fragment and travel through the aorta to these organs, explaining the abrupt flank pain, hematuria, and splenic hypodensity.

explanation_incorrect.A: Immune complex deposition is the mechanism of the immunologic phenomena of endocarditis, such as glomerulonephritis with hematuria, but it produces diffuse glomerular inflammation, not a wedge-shaped splenic infarct on CT.
explanation_incorrect.B: Infection does not spread retrograde through the renal vein to the spleen; the pattern here is arterial embolization from the left heart.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mycotic (infectious) aneurysms of arteries can complicate endocarditis, but the CT shows a wedge-shaped hypodensity typical of infarction, not a ruptured aneurysm with hemorrhage.
explanation_incorrect.E: Direct extension of infection through the pericardium would involve the myocardium or pericardial space adjacent to the heart, not distant organs such as the spleen reached only via the bloodstream.

educationalObjective: Left-sided infective endocarditis produces septic emboli to the systemic circulation (spleen, kidney, brain), whereas right-sided disease embolizes to the lungs.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 51-year-old woman with subacute infective endocarditis undergoes ophthalmologic evaluation for blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows bilateral retinal hemorrhages with pale, whitish centers. She also has painful, raised, violaceous nodules on the pads of her right index finger and a new apical systolic murmur.
question: The retinal findings observed in this patient represent which type of endocarditis phenomenon?

options.text: Vascular phenomenon caused by septic embolization to the retina
Immunologic phenomenon caused by immune complex deposition
Direct invasion of the retina by low-virulence streptococci
Adverse effect of empiric vancomycin therapy
Hypertensive retinopathy unrelated to the endocarditis

explanation_correct: Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers are Roth spots, an immunologic phenomenon of infective endocarditis caused by immune complex deposition. They accompany other immunologic findings such as glomerulonephritis and Osler nodes, which this patient also has (the painful raised violaceous nodules on the finger pads, classically "Ouchy" Osler nodes). Together with fever and a new murmur, these findings complete the classic clinical picture.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vascular phenomena include septic embolism, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, and Janeway lesions; Roth spots are classified with the immunologic phenomena because they arise from immune complex deposition rather than embolic seeding of organisms.
explanation_incorrect.C: Roth spots are not due to direct microbial invasion of the retina; the pale center represents immune complexes and fibrin, which is why they are grouped with immunologic findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Vancomycin can cause ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and flushing (red man syndrome), not retinal hemorrhages with pale centers.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypertensive retinopathy produces arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, and flame hemorrhages without the characteristic pale-centered hemorrhage of Roth spots, and this vignette explicitly attributes the ocular findings to the patient's endocarditis context.

educationalObjective: Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages with pale centers) and Osler nodes are immunologic phenomena of infective endocarditis caused by immune complex deposition.
